Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity, 
diabetes mellitus and retinopathy: an anti-GAD 
syndrome

A 59-year-old woman with a past history of pigmentary retinopathy developed progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity 
(PEW) characterized clinically by cerebellar ataxia, pyramidal signs and stiffness with painful muscle spasms. At the same 
period, retinopathy strikingly worsened. Her serum contained antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (CAD). She 
developed diabetes mellitus under corticotherapy, which was inefficient. Neurologic signs dramatically improved with 
diazepam and high dose of intravenous immunoglobulin (i.v. Ig). AntlGAD antibodies have been described In stiN man 
syndrome, but in only one previous case of PEWR Presence of such autoantibodies in serum and improvement following 1.v. 
IgC infusion strongly suggest an autoimmune mechanism Involving, in our case central nervous system, pancreas and 
probably retina.

immunoglobulin 
Stiff man syndrome (SMS) and progressive encephalo- 
myelitis with rigidity (PEWR) are very rare central ner- 
vous system (CNS) disorders with continuous muscle 
activity reversible with GABAergic therapy (Thompson, 
1993). SMS has been linked to the production of anti- 
glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies (Nemni, 
1994; Solimena er al., 1988), a finding mentioned in only 
one previous case of PEWR (Burn el al., 1991). Here, we 
report on a new case of PEWR in which a seric anti-GAD 
activity was demonstrated. Both entities may result from 
autoimmunity against GABA-ergic neurons. 
CLINICAL HISTORY 
A 59-year-old black woman presented in March 1993 
with a 5 months progression of gait disturbance with 
repetitive falls and painful muscle spasms in the four 
limbs that reached the axial musculature. She had a recent 
history of hemeralopia due to a proved retinitis pigmen- 
tosa. Neurological examination showed a diffised perma- 
nent stiffness with lumber hyperlordosis. sparing only the 
face. The superimposed spasms appeared spontaneously 
98 European Jod of Neurology . Vol3 . 1996 
or were triggered by unexpected noises. The patient was 
unable to walk because of stiffness and marked cerebellar 
ataxia. There were diffise hyperreflexia with bilateral 
Babinski sign. Examination was otherwise unremarkable. 
CT scan of the head was normal as well as MRI of brain 
and spinal cord. Creatine phospho kinase (CPK) was 
increased to 408 UIA (normal up to 90 UVI), Ig G level 
in serum was 23% (normal up to 20%). Serologies for 
human retro-viruses (IIIV I, HTLV 1) were negative. The 
following antibodies were present: anti-smooth muscle at 
1/640 and anti-cardiolipines at 70 UIA (normal up to 
Serological studies for anti-microsomal, anti-parietal 
cell, anti-mitochondrial, and anti-thyroglobulin antibo-

dies yielded negative results. HLA typing was as follows: 
Aw 19, A3, B44, Bw 41. Concentric needle electromyo- 
graphy showed continuous muscle activity in the right 
biceps brachialis and extensor carpi radialis longus and 
paraspinal cervical muscles. NO fasciculations, fibrilla- 
tions or myokymias were seen. SSEPs showed decreased 
amplitudes with normal latencies for medullary respon- 
ses. An electroencephalogram was normal. Cerebrospinal 
fluid (CSF) examination was normal for cell count, giu-

without oligoclonal bands. A thorough survey of malig- 
nant markers (ACE, AFP, CA 15.3, CA 19.9, CT scan of 
the chest, intra-venous urogram, anti-HU, anti-Yo, anti- 
CAR antibodies) was negative. A muscle biopsy was 
normal. 
METHODS 
Anti-GAD antibodies were detected in serum by ELISA 
using as antigens human recombinant GAD 65 and GAD 
67, expressed in a eukaryotic system (Baculovirus in 
system SF 9). The antigens were kindly provided by 
ELIAS (Molecular Biology Department, Freibourg, Ger- 
many). Western Blot using the same recombinant anti- 
gens was also performed. Immunofluorescence was 
carried out on cryostat sections of human pancreas and 
monkey cerebellum. 
RESULTS 
Immunological studies 
The following results were obtained by ELISA with the 
patient serum: anti-GAD 67 (GAD I) patient serum: 
200 U/ml (normal sera, n = 460: 1.6 U/ml f 4.7), anti- 
GAD 65 (GAD 11) patient serum: 7000 Wml (normal 
sera, n = 1592: 490 UVml f 1171) (Fig. 1). In Western 
Blot, only GAD 65 was recognized by the patient serum. 
In pancreas, a strong fluorescence signal was observed, 
but restricted to B cells. 
The specificity was demonstrated by double staining 
technique using anti-glucagon and anti-GAD 65 mono- 
clonal antibodies. On monkey cerebellum, GABA-ergic 
nerve terminals within the molecular layer and at the base 
of the Purkinje cells were stained (Fig. 2). 
Response to treatment 
Under diazepam (40 mg daily), painful muscle jerks and 
diffuse stiffness completely disappeared. However, ataxia 
and visual condition continued to worsen. Successive 
trials of corticotherapy, which induced diabetes mellitus, 
cyclophosphamide and azathioprine were unsuccessful. 
In October 1993, the patient was confined to a wheel- 
chair, visual acuity had severely deteriorated leading to 
blindness. No electroretinogram recording was canied 
out. From that time, the patient was given monthly in- 
travenous immunoglobulin (i.v. Ig) therapy (0.4 g/kg/day 
for 5 consecutive days). Following the first cure, a dra-

matic improvement was observed. After the fourth cure 
of i.v. Ig, she was able to walk unaided and following the 
sixth i.v. Ig, she reduced diazepam dosage by 30 mg 
without recurrence of rigidity. Her ambulation at home 
was only impaired by persistent blindness. This clinical

DISCUSSION 
SMS is a rare central nervous system (CNS) disease 
Characterized clinically by permanent muscle rigidity and 
painful spasms. Electromyography reveals continuous 
motorunit activity in the affected muscles (Thompson, 
1993). These findings were observed in our case, but 
additional involvement of pyramidal tract and cerebellar 
ataxia were indicative of PEWR rather than SMS. 
Only few similar cases of PEWR have been previously 
described (Bateman et al., 1990; Bum et al., 199 1 ; Ca- 
sad0 er ul.. 1994: Howell el ul., 1979; McCombe er ul., 
1989; Whitely el al., 1976). In this disorder, rigidity of 
SMS type was associated with other CNS signs such as 
sensory disturbances (Bum el al., 199 1 ; McCombe er al., 
1989). weakness (Bateman et a[., 1990; Darnell el (11.. 
1993; Whitely el a/.. 1976). nystagmus (Bum el al., 
199 1 ; Casado et al., 1994), ophthalmoplegia (Bateman 
er of., 1990; Howell et al., 1979), dysarthria (Bateman ef 
100 European Joumal of Neurology . Vol3 . 1996 
a/., 1990; Whitely et al., 1976), ataxia (Howell et al., 
1979) and myoclonus (Casado el al., 1994). PEWR 
usually progressed into death within a few years. Post 
mortem examination consistently showed encephalomye- 
litis, mainly affecting the brainstem and cervical spinal 
cord (Burn el al., 1991; Howell el al., 1979). Little is 
known about the pathophysiologic nature of this disorder. 
Similar clinical and electrophysiological features shared 
by SMS and PEWR could reflect the same mechanism. 
Occasionally, a remote effect of malignancy was estab- 
lished (Burn et al., 1991; Folli et al., 1993), a possibility 
excluded in our case by negative workup for neoplasm 
and clinical course. Anti-GAD antibodies have been 
found in up to 60% of SMS patients (Brashear and Phil- 
lips, 1991; Darnell ef al., 1993; Solimena et a/., 1988, 
I990), suggesting an auto-immune-mediated dysfunction 
of GABA-ergic pathways controlling motor activity. In 
our PEWR patient, a body of data strongly suggests that 
the same pathogenesis is involved. That includes the pre- 
sence of haplotype 844 which is linked to SMS (Thornp- 
son, 1993), the intrathecal synthesis of Ig G and 
especially the finding of anti-GAD antibodies, which was 
described in only one previous case report of PEWR 
(Bateman et ai., 1990). Furthermore, cells containing 
GAD in cerebellum and in pancreas were strongly 
stained. In view of these findings, we postulate that in

our patient anti-GAD antibodies induced rigidity, ataxia 
and latent diabetes mellitus. Retinopathy which worsened 
in parallel to ataxia might also be triggered by anti-GAD 
activity. 
Th~s hypothesis is also supported by the recent demon- 
stration of a large amount of GABAcontaining neurons 
in the inner nuclear layer of retina (Versaux-Botteri et al., 
1994; Yu et al., 1988). We therefore suggest that anti- 
GAD antibodies might be implicated in a wider spectrum 
of clinical syndromes. For instance, Nemni et al. (1994) 
recently reported presence of anti-GAD activity in a pa- 
tient with palatal myoclonus, which authors surmised was 
due to involvement of GABAergic pathway controlling 
inferior olivary nuclei activity. The immunological pat- 
tern observed in our PEWR patient, consisting in higher 
titer of anti-GAD 65 than anti-GAD 67 in ELISA and in 
selective recognition of GAD 65 by serum tested in Wes- 
tern-blotting, is identical to this of SMS patients (Butler 
et al., 1993) and therefore do not distinguish PEWR from 
SMS. 
Intravenous Ig strikingly improved ataxia and permit- 
ted reduction of the patient’s diazepam intake, but failed 
to restore any vision. Whether the loss of retina GABA- 
ergic cells was too severe to allow response to therapy, 
remains questionable. The neurological improvement in 
our patient under i.v. Ig suggests that immunoglobulins 
affect the production and action of anti-GAD antibodies 
(Amato et al., 1994; Karlson et al., 1994) in the CNS and 
strengthens the auto-immune hypothesis concerning 
PEWR.
